subject: economics
promptStrong: Give me a challenging GCSE exam-style question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the AQA spec.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for GCSE AQA Economics simply, with an example and the most common mistake.
learningObjectives: economic foundations, factors of production and opportunity cost
resource allocation, specialisation and the division of labour
demand, supply and how prices are determined
price elasticity of demand and supply
competitive and concentrated markets and the labour market
market failure, externalities and government intervention

questions.lo: economic foundations, factors of production and opportunity cost
questions.q: Which set correctly lists the four factors of production?
questions.explain: The four factors of production are land (natural resources), labour (human effort), capital (man-made aids to production) and enterprise (organising the other factors and taking risk). Money is not a factor of production.

questions.lo: economic foundations, factors of production and opportunity cost
questions.q: A government spends £2bn on a new hospital instead of on schools. The opportunity cost of the hospital is:
options: The number of patients treated in the hospital
The extra tax needed to fund it
The schools that could have been built with that £2bn
questions.explain: Opportunity cost is the value of the next best alternative given up when a choice is made. Here that is the schools forgone, not the money itself.

questions.lo: economic foundations, factors of production and opportunity cost
questions.q: The reward that accrues to the factor of production 'enterprise' is:
questions.explain: Land earns rent, labour earns wages, capital earns interest and enterprise earns profit as its reward for risk-taking and organising production.

questions.lo: resource allocation, specialisation and the division of labour
questions.q: In economics, a market is best defined as:
options: A firm that has no competitors
An opportunity for buyers and sellers to interact to establish a price
A place where the government sets prices
questions.explain: A market is any arrangement that brings buyers and sellers together so a price can be established; it need not be a physical place.

questions.lo: resource allocation, specialisation and the division of labour
questions.q: Extracting crude oil from an oil field is an example of activity in which sector?
questions.explain: The primary sector extracts raw materials (e.g. mining, farming, fishing). Manufacturing is secondary and services are tertiary.

questions.lo: resource allocation, specialisation and the division of labour
questions.q: Which is a drawback of the division of labour for a worker?
options: Firms can train workers more quickly
Time is saved switching between tasks
Output per worker tends to rise
Work can become repetitive and boring, lowering motivation
questions.explain: Specialisation raises productivity but can make tasks monotonous, reducing worker motivation and job satisfaction. The other options are benefits, not costs.

questions.lo: demand, supply and how prices are determined
questions.q: A rise in the price of a good, with all else unchanged, causes:
options: A shift of the whole demand curve to the right
A shift of the whole demand curve to the left
No change in the quantity demanded
A movement up along the demand curve (a contraction of demand)
questions.explain: A change in the good's own price causes a movement ALONG the demand curve (a contraction). Only a change in a non-price factor shifts the whole curve.

questions.lo: demand, supply and how prices are determined
questions.q: Which non-price factor would shift the demand curve for beef to the RIGHT?
options: A fall in the cost of raising cattle
A successful advertising campaign making beef more popular
A rise in the price of beef
questions.explain: Advertising that increases tastes/popularity raises demand at every price, shifting the curve right. A fall in the cost of raising cattle shifts SUPPLY, not demand, and a price rise is a movement along the curve.

questions.lo: demand, supply and how prices are determined
questions.q: A new technology lowers firms' production costs. On the supply-and-demand diagram this causes:
options: The demand curve to shift right
The supply curve to shift right, lowering equilibrium price and raising quantity
The supply curve to shift left, raising equilibrium price
A movement along the supply curve only
questions.explain: Lower costs make firms willing to supply more at each price, shifting supply right. This creates a new equilibrium at a lower price and higher quantity.

questions.lo: demand, supply and how prices are determined
questions.q: At a price above the equilibrium price, a market will typically show:
options: Excess demand (a shortage), pushing price up
Excess supply (a surplus), pushing price down
No trade taking place at all
questions.explain: Above equilibrium, quantity supplied exceeds quantity demanded, creating a surplus. Firms cut prices to clear stock, so price falls back towards equilibrium.

questions.lo: price elasticity of demand and supply
questions.q: Price elasticity of demand (PED) is calculated as:
options: % change in price divided by % change in quantity demanded
Total revenue divided by total cost
% change in quantity demanded divided by % change in price
Change in quantity demanded minus change in price
questions.explain: PED = percentage change in quantity demanded / percentage change in price. It measures how responsive quantity demanded is to a price change.

questions.lo: price elasticity of demand and supply
questions.q: The price of a good rises by 10% and quantity demanded falls by 4%. Demand is:
questions.explain: PED = 4% / 10% = 0.4. Because the value is less than 1, demand is price inelastic: quantity demanded changes proportionately less than price.

questions.lo: price elasticity of demand and supply
questions.q: Which good is most likely to have price INELASTIC demand?
options: A life-saving prescription medicine with no substitute
One particular airline on a busy competitive route
A brand of chocolate bar with many close substitutes
questions.explain: A necessity with no substitutes has inelastic demand: consumers keep buying it even if the price rises. Goods with many substitutes tend to be elastic.

questions.lo: production, costs, revenue and profit
questions.q: Profit is correctly defined as:
questions.explain: Profit = total revenue - total costs. A firm can raise profit by increasing revenue and/or reducing average costs.

questions.lo: production, costs, revenue and profit
questions.q: A firm sells 500 units at £8 each, with total costs of £3,000. Its total revenue and profit are:
questions.explain: Total revenue = price x quantity = £8 x 500 = £4,000. Profit = revenue - costs = £4,000 - £3,000 = £1,000.

questions.lo: production, costs, revenue and profit
questions.q: Which best describes the difference between production and productivity?
options: They mean exactly the same thing
Production measures profit; productivity measures revenue
Productivity is total output; production is output per worker
Production is total output; productivity is output per unit of input (e.g. per worker)
questions.explain: Production is the total amount produced. Productivity measures efficiency: output per unit of input, such as output per worker per hour. Higher productivity can lower average costs.

questions.lo: production, costs, revenue and profit
questions.q: A large supermarket chain can buy stock more cheaply per unit than a small corner shop. This is an example of:
questions.explain: Buying in bulk to secure lower unit prices is a purchasing economy of scale, one way large firms achieve lower average costs as output rises.

questions.lo: competitive and concentrated markets and the labour market
questions.q: A market dominated by a single producer with no close competitors is a:
questions.explain: A monopoly exists where one firm dominates the market. An oligopoly is a market dominated by a few large firms; competitive markets have many firms.

questions.lo: competitive and concentrated markets and the labour market
questions.q: Compared with a monopoly, a highly competitive market tends to lead to:
options: Higher prices and less choice for consumers
No effect on price or choice
Guaranteed higher profits for every firm
Lower prices, more choice and lower profits for firms
questions.explain: Competition puts downward pressure on prices, widens consumer choice and tends to squeeze firms' profits, whereas a monopoly can charge higher prices.

questions.lo: market failure, externalities and government intervention
questions.q: A factory pollutes a river, harming people downstream who are not involved in the transaction. This is an example of:
questions.explain: Pollution imposes a cost on third parties, so social cost exceeds private cost. This is a negative externality, a form of market failure the government may correct through taxes or regulation.
